newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Commission proposes extending worker consultation rules.
newsitem.headline: Commission proposes extending worker consultation rules.

text.p: The European Commission said on Monday it planned to ask labour unions and employers to negotiate rules to require national companies in the European Union to set up procedures for consulting their workers.

The initiative would complement the EU Works Council directive, 94/45/EC, which already obliges multinational companies to set up systems for informing and consulting employees about important developments.
Social Affairs Commissioner Padraig Flynn intends to present the new plan to the Social Affairs Council on Tuesday, Commission spokeswoman Barbara Nolan told a news briefing.
Flynn will propose that an accord be negotiated under the EU's Social Protocol, from which Britain has an opt out.
He decided to act after getting positive feedback from most EU states on the need for a European initiative in this area, Nolan said.

At the same time, the Commission has been unable to break a longstanding deadlock between EU states over a related proposal to allow firms to set up as "European companies" and will propose that it be referred to a group of experts, she said.

The European Company Statute -- along with proposals for a European association, European cooperative society and European mutual society -- has been blocked for many years by a dispute between EU states over provisions on worker participation.
Germany has fought to apply its own system of "co-determination" for workers, while Britain wants no mandatory rules.

But Commission proposals for breaking the impasse have met with opposition, especially from Germany, because they would apply general EU rules on worker "consultation" -- rather than "participation" -- to the new entities.

EU member states -- who are coming under increasing pressure to agree the European Company Statute -- generally support the idea of referring the question to a group of high-level experts, EU officials said.
EU trade unions and employers have negotiated one accord under the Social Protocol so far, covering parental and family leave, which was then turned into EU law by the Council.
